title: Got your building's SIRS? How to read it in 15 minutes, page by page
seoTitle: How to Read Your Florida Condo SIRS Report
description: A Florida condo SIRS can run dozens of pages. Here is what the law says must be in it, the five parts to find first, and the questions to ask your board.
dek: The structural integrity reserve study is the report behind your reserve bill. It looks long and technical, but Florida law says what it must contain. Here are the five parts to find first, and what to ask once you have.

body.text: Many Florida condo owners now have a copy of their building's structural integrity reserve study, or a notice saying they can ask for one. It can look like a stack of spreadsheets and engineering terms. The good news: Florida law says what the study must contain. Once you know the parts, you can find what matters in about 15 minutes.
This is a reading guide, not legal or engineering advice. For questions about your building, ask the board, the association attorney, or the professional who prepared the study.

body.title: Terms to know
body.text: SIRS: the structural integrity reserve study. Florida law requires one at least every 10 years for each condo building three or more habitable stories tall. Reserves: money the association saves for big future repairs and replacements. Remaining useful life: how many more years an item is expected to last. Deferred maintenance: repair work that has been put off and will have to be paid for later.
What the law says a SIRS must contain

Section 718.112(2)(g) of the 2026 Florida Statutes sets the rules. The study is based on a visual inspection of the property. It must be performed or verified by a Florida-licensed engineer or architect, or by a certified reserve specialist or professional reserve analyst.
At a minimum, the study covers these items:

items: The roof.
The structure, including load-bearing walls and primary structural members and systems.
Fireproofing and fire protection systems.
Plumbing.
Electrical systems.
Waterproofing and exterior painting.
Windows and exterior doors.
Any other item with a deferred maintenance expense or replacement cost of more than $25,000 (or the higher inflation-adjusted amount the state sets) whose failure would hurt the items above.

body.text: For each item, the law says the study must give its estimated remaining useful life and its estimated replacement cost or deferred maintenance expense. It must also give a reserve funding plan or schedule with a recommended annual reserve amount.
The five parts to find first
Every preparer lays out the report a little differently. But because of what the law requires, these five things should be in there somewhere. Grab a pen and look for them in this order.

items: 1. Who prepared it and when. Near the front, find the preparer's name, licence or credential, and the date of the visual inspection. This tells you how fresh the numbers are.

2. The list of items. Check that the roof, structure, fire protection, plumbing, electrical, waterproofing and painting, and windows and exterior doors all appear. If an item is missing or marked as excluded, note it and ask why. The law lets some items be left out, for example when their useful life or cost cannot be determined.
3. The years-left column. Look for remaining useful life next to each item. Circle anything with only a few years left. Those are the bills coming soonest.
4. The cost column. Next to each item, find the estimated replacement cost or deferred maintenance expense. Big numbers next to small years-left numbers are the ones to ask about.
5. The recommended yearly amount. Find the funding plan or schedule and the recommended annual reserve amount. This is the number that feeds into your share of the budget.

body.text: The baseline funding plan, in plain words

The law says the study must include a recommendation based on a baseline funding plan. Under that plan, the reserve cash balance stays above zero in every budget year, and each item's reserves are fully funded by the end of its remaining useful life. Think of it as the minimum plan that never lets the savings account hit empty.

The study may also recommend other funding schedules, as long as each one is enough to meet the association's maintenance duties. So you may see more than one plan side by side. Ask the board which one the budget follows.

The study must also consider how the association plans to pay: regular assessments, special assessments, lines of credit or loans. If the funding method changes, the law says the study must be updated.
How the SIRS connects to your budget

Section 718.112(2)(f) says the reserve amount for the SIRS items must be based on the findings and recommendations of the most recent study. For unit-owner-controlled associations, budgets adopted on or after December 31, 2024 may not provide no reserves or less reserves for those items. There are narrow exceptions, such as a temporary pause for up to two budget years after a milestone inspection, which takes a vote of a majority of the total voting interests (more than half of all the votes in the association, not just those at the meeting).
That is why the recommended yearly amount in the study matters so much. It is a big part of why reserve bills have gone up.
What the association must do once it gets the study

items: Within 45 days of receiving the study, the association must give each owner a copy, or give notice that a copy is available on written request. It can be sent by mail, by hand, or electronically to owners who agreed to electronic notice.

Also within 45 days, the association must tell the state's Division of Florida Condominiums, Timeshares and Mobile Homes that the study was completed and provided or made available to owners. DBPR's page says associations do this with a SIRS Reporting Form in their online account.
Officers or directors must sign an affidavit saying they received the completed study.

body.text: What to do
If you are an owner:

items: If you got a notice instead of the study, ask for a copy in writing. Keep a copy of your request.
Do the five-part check above. Write down every item with few years left and a large cost.
Ask the board which funding plan the proposed budget follows, and whether a special assessment, loan or line of credit is being considered for any item.
Check whether your association's SIRS report shows up on DBPR's public SIRS lists. Search "SIRS reporting" on myfloridalicense.com. DBPR says only complete submissions are shown.

body.text: If you serve on the board:

items: Mark the 45-day clock on your calendar the day the study arrives, for both owner delivery and the DBPR report.
Ask the preparer to walk the board and owners through the items, the years left, the costs and the recommended amount at an open meeting.
Ask the preparer to explain any excluded items and any plan other than the baseline plan in writing.

Have the association attorney confirm how the budget's reserves match the study before the budget is adopted. DBPR's condo division can answer reporting questions at ctmheducation@myfloridalicense.com or (954) 202-6831.

faq.q: What is in a structural integrity reserve study in Florida?
faq.a: Section 718.112(2)(g) says it covers at least the roof, structure, fire protection, plumbing, electrical, waterproofing and exterior painting, windows and exterior doors, and certain other items over $25,000. For each item it gives the remaining useful life and the estimated cost, plus a funding plan with a recommended yearly reserve amount.

faq.q: Does my condo have to give me a copy of the SIRS?
faq.a: Within 45 days of receiving the study, the association must give each owner a copy, or give notice that a copy is available on written request. If you got a notice, ask for the copy in writing.

faq.q: What is a baseline funding plan in a SIRS?
faq.a: It is the plan the law requires the study to recommend. Under it, the reserve cash balance stays above zero every budget year, and each item is fully funded by the end of its remaining useful life. The study may show other plans too.

faq.q: How do I check if my condo reported its SIRS to the state?
faq.a: DBPR's Division of Florida Condominiums, Timeshares and Mobile Homes posts public lists of SIRS reporting forms on myfloridalicense.com. Search "SIRS reporting." DBPR says only complete submissions are displayed, and online submissions should appear within one business day.

faq.q: Who can prepare a SIRS in Florida?
faq.a: The study must be performed or verified by a Florida-licensed engineer or architect, or by a certified reserve specialist or professional reserve analyst.
